sections.b: The prayer praises God as maker of heaven and earth who put the sea in fetters and sealed the abyss with his name (verses 1–4); his anger is past bearing but his mercy past measuring, for he is "slow to anger and great in mercy" (verses 5–7). Repentance, it says, was not set for the righteous patriarchs but "for me, the sinner" (verse 8). The king confesses sins beyond the sand of the sea, bent low by a heavy iron chain (verses 9–10), bends "my heart's knee" (verse 11), and begs to be let go and spared (verses 12–14), promising lifelong praise (verse 15).

Chronicles says Manasseh's prayer in captivity was written down (2 Chronicles 33:18–19) but does not give it. A Greek prayer of fifteen verses in his name fills the gap. It is found among the odes after the Psalms in Codex Alexandrinus and in the Apostolic Constitutions (book 2, section 22), which add that after he prayed, a flame of fire surrounded him and his iron shackles fell off. The prayer speaks of "a heavy iron chain" (Prayer of Manasseh 10), where Chronicles has "bronze fetters" (2 Chronicles 33:11). Orthodox churches read it at Great Compline, mostly in Lent; Article VI of the Church of England lists it among the books read "for example of life."

claude.title: The army he worshiped sings to God
claude.body: Manasseh "bowed down to all the army of the heavens" (2 Chronicles 33:3). The prayer in his name ends with "the whole army of the heavens" singing hymns to God (Prayer of Manasseh 15). Claude suggests the writer chose the phrase to show the king's worship set right; no source opened for this page says so.

sections.h: Repentance set for sinners (Prayer of Manasseh)
sections.b: The Prayer of Manasseh plays on one Greek root. God is the one who "changes his mind" (literally "repents") about harm (Prayer of Manasseh 7, the formula of Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2); he did not set repentance for the righteous but "for me, the sinner" (Prayer of Manasseh 8); and he is "the God of those who repent" (Prayer of Manasseh 13). Jesus' sayings in Luke use the same Greek words: "I have come to call sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32; compare Luke 15:7).
sections.refs: Prayer of Manasseh 7–8; Prayer of Manasseh 13; Joel 2:13; Luke 5:32; Luke 15:7

common: The Prayer of Manasseh is read as a model of repentance by Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians, who keep it in their Bibles or Apocrypha.

sections.b: The Prayer of Manasseh's most famous line, "Now I bend my heart's knee" (Prayer of Manasseh 11), moves kneeling, a posture of prayer (1 Kings 8:54), inward: a man bent by a chain kneels inside. 1 Clement uses the same picture, "bending the knees of your hearts" (1 Clement 57:1). The prayer is read in the Orthodox service of Great Compline in Lent, after Psalm 51 and Psalm 102.

The Prayer of Manasseh sets God's two sides side by side: "no one can stand against your anger when you threaten sinners," but "the mercy you promise is past measuring and past searching out" (Prayer of Manasseh 5–6). It then quotes the creed of Exodus 34:6 in the form of Joel and Jonah: "slow to anger and great in mercy" (Prayer of Manasseh 7). The plea rests on that mercy alone: "You will save me, though I am unworthy, as your mercy is great" (Prayer of Manasseh 14; compare Psalm 51:1).
sections.refs: Prayer of Manasseh 5–7; Prayer of Manasseh 14; Exodus 34:6; Joel 2:13; Psalm 51:1

sections.b: In the Prayer of Manasseh the plea for forgiveness is a plea to be untied. The Greek anes moi, "let me go," is from the verb "loosen"; the chained king has "no relief" (a loosening, Prayer of Manasseh 10) and begs, "let me go free, Lord, let me go free" (Prayer of Manasseh 13). The KJV Apocrypha renders it "forgive me."
sections.refs: Prayer of Manasseh 10; Prayer of Manasseh 13

sections.b: The Prayer of Manasseh measures sin with Abraham's blessing: God promised offspring like "the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17); the king has sinned "beyond the count of the sand of the sea" (Prayer of Manasseh 9). It calls the patriarchs those "who had not sinned against you" (Prayer of Manasseh 8), a contrast drawn more sharply than Genesis draws it (Genesis 12:11–13; Genesis 27:18–24).

The Prayer of Manasseh sums up the long list of 2 Chronicles 33:3–7 in two lines: "I set up abhorrent things and heaped up things you loathe" (Prayer of Manasseh 10). Both Greek words, bdelygmata and prosochthismata, are Greek Bible words for idols and the practices that go with them.

Kings tells no repentance of Manasseh (2 Kings 21); Chronicles does (2 Chronicles 33:10–16) and says his prayer was written down (2 Chronicles 33:18–19). The Prayer of Manasseh, kept in Greek, supplies the words of that prayer, so it belongs to Chronicles' version of the story.

sections.h: The Prayer of Manasseh: in, out, and in between
sections.b: Few books show the edges of the canon as clearly as the Prayer of Manasseh. Orthodox churches read it in worship and count it among their Old Testament books. The Council of Trent's list leaves it out, and the Clementine Vulgate put it after the New Testament, saying it "exists neither in Hebrew nor even in Greek" and is part of no canonical book, though it does survive in Greek. Article VI of the Church of England lists it among the books read for life and manners but not for doctrine; Luther kept it among the Apocrypha; the Westminster Confession counts no Apocrypha as Scripture. It is not in the Jewish Bible.

sections.h: Lord Almighty, God of those who repent
sections.b: The Prayer of Manasseh opens with "Lord Almighty in heaven, God of our fathers" (Prayer of Manasseh 1) and calls God "the Lord Most High" (Prayer of Manasseh 7) and "God of the righteous" (Prayer of Manasseh 8). It closes with a new title for God: "the God of those who repent" (Prayer of Manasseh 13). The abyss is sealed "with your fearsome and glorious name" (Prayer of Manasseh 3).

sections.b: The Prayer of Manasseh praises God who "put the sea in fetters" and "shut the abyss and sealed it with your fearsome and glorious name" (Prayer of Manasseh 3), the picture of the deep held back by God's command (Job 38:8–11) that Revelation uses when an angel shuts and seals the abyss over the dragon (Revelation 20:3).
